sources.title: Forecast for Overlord: June 6, 1944
sources.citation: Stagg, J. M. (1971). Forecast for Overlord, June 6, 1944. W. W. Norton & Company.
sources.supported_claim: Stagg's own account, as Eisenhower's chief meteorologist, of the forecasting process, the disagreement among British and American forecasting teams, and the content of the briefings given to Eisenhower on June 4-5, 1944.

sources.title: How a weather forecast made history - the D-Day Landings
sources.supported_claim: Technical account of 1944 forecasting limitations (no satellite data, reliance on ship/land observation networks) and the genuine uncertainty in the June 4-5 forecast.

sources.title: How The D-Day Landings Were Delayed By A Weather Forecast
sources.supported_claim: Timeline of the June 4 postponement from the originally planned June 5 date and the Southwick House decision process leading to the June 5 go order.

sources.title: Pressure, the D-Day Weather Forecast Story
sources.author_or_institution: The National WWII Museum, New Orleans
sources.supported_claim: Narrative account of the Southwick House meetings, Stagg's forecast delivery, and Eisenhower's decision process and approximate timing.

sources.title: General Dwight D. Eisenhower's Order of the Day (1944)
sources.date: Document dated June 1944; archive record ongoing
sources.supported_claim: Primary document context for Eisenhower's authority and framing of the invasion decision; used to cross-check the decision's timing and framing.

sources.title: D-Day, 'OK, we'll go'
sources.supported_claim: Account of Eisenhower's own description of the decision moment, including the pause before giving the final order, sourced to Eisenhower's own later writings.

sources.title: The Mulberries Battle the Storm -- June 19, 1944
sources.author_or_institution: Old Salt Blog (naval history specialist publication), corroborated by Naval History and Heritage Command Mulberry harbor records
sources.supported_claim: Account of the severe June 19, 1944 Channel storm that destroyed the Omaha Beach Mulberry harbor (Mulberry A), used to support the unknown_at_t0 claim about what the alternative ~June 19 window would have brought.

sources.title: D-Day: Mulberries
sources.author_or_institution: Naval History and Heritage Command, US Navy
sources.supported_claim: Official US Navy record confirming the scale of the June 19, 1944 storm damage to the Mulberry harbors (21 of 28 caissons destroyed at Mulberry A).

sources.title: Normandy landings
sources.supported_claim: General chronology cross-check of the invasion date, scale, and immediate/long-term outcome.
